## Introduction ### Learning goals In this session, you will learn additional Unix shell skills, focusing on commands to manage files with an eye on organizing your research projects. Specifically, you will learn about: - **Command substitution** to save the output of commands - **For loops** to repeat operations, e.g. across files - **Renaming multiple files** using for loops
### Getting ready ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} #### Starting VS Code at OSC - with a Terminal *(Click to expand)* TBA :::
### Create a dummy project folder structure Go into the dir for this week that you created earlier: ```sh # You should be in /fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER/ cd week03 ``` First, we'll create a set of directories representing a dummy research project: ```sh mkdir dummy-project cd dummy-project ``` ```sh # The -p option for mkdir will allow for 'recursive' (nested) dir creation mkdir -p data/fastq scripts results/figures results/alignments ``` We will use the `touch` command to create empty files that are mock representations of FASTQ sequence files with forward ("R1") and reverse ("R2") DNA sequence reads for 3 samples: ```sh # (Copy-and-paste this rather than typing it out) touch data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq data/fastq/sample1_R2.fastq touch data/fastq/sample2_R1.fastq data/fastq/sample2_R2.fastq touch data/fastq/sample3_R1.fastq data/fastq/sample3_R2.fastq ``` For a nice recursive overview of the project directory structure you just created, use the **`tree` command** (with option `-C` to show colors): ```bash # (Output colors are not shown on this webpage) tree -C ``` ```bash-out ../.. ├── data │ └── fastq │ ├── sample1_R1.fastq │ ├── sample1_R2.fastq │ ├── sample2_R1.fastq │ ├── sample2_R2.fastq │ ├── sample3_R1.fastq │ └── sample3_R2.fastq ├── results │ └── figures └── scripts 5 directories, 6 files ```
::: callout-note #### More shell keyboard shortcuts - **Ctrl+U** cuts text until the beginning of the line. - **Ctrl+Y** "yanks" the cut text back - **Alt+.** (or **Esc+.** on a Mac) will insert the last word (argument) from the last command line (and you can cycle back by pressing it multiple times!). - When you hold Ctrl and press the arrow buttons, you will move word-by-word rather than character-by-character. - You can also cut (delete) word-by-word by pressing Ctrl+W or Alt+Backspace (=Option+Delete). :::
## Variables and command substitution Now, we'll cover a few topics that do not directly relate to files, but that you need to know about before the application at the end of this session: renaming files with a loop. Additionally, you will keep using these constructs throughout the course. ### Variables Variables are truly ubiquitous in programming. We typically use them for items that: - We refer to repeatedly and/or - Are subject to change. These tend to be _settings_ like the paths to input and output files, and parameter values for programs. **Using variables makes it easier to change such settings and makes it possible** **to write scripts and programs that are flexible depending on user input.** Earlier, we already saw a couple of handy applications of variables: for example, the environment variable `$USER` contains our user name. #### Assigning and referencing variables To **assign** a value to a variable in the shell, use the syntax `variable_name=value`: ```bash # Assign the value "beach" to a variable with the name "location": location=beach # Assign the value "200" to a variable with the name "nr_samples": nr_samples=200 ``` :::{.callout-warning} ##### Note that there can't be spaces around the equals sign (`=`)! ::: To **reference** a variable (i.e., to access its value): - You need to put a dollar sign `$` in front of its name. - It is good practice to double-quote (`"..."`) variable names^[ We'll talk more about quoting later.]. As before with the environment variables `$USER` and `$HOME`, we'll use the `echo` command to see what values our variables contain: ```bash echo "$location" ``` ```{.bash-out} beach ``` ```bash echo "$nr_samples" ``` ```{.bash-out} 200 ``` Conveniently, we can use variables in lots of contexts, _as if we had directly typed their values_: ```bash input_file=data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq ls -lh "$input_file" ``` ```{.bash-out} -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 0 Mar 7 13:17 data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq ``` ::: {.callout-info collapse="true"} #### Compared with R syntax - Assigning and printing the value of a variable **in R**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # (Don't run this) x <- 5 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` styled-output [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: ```bash-out [1] 5 ``` - Assigning and printing the value of a variable **in the Unix shell**: ``` bash x=5 echo $x ``` ``` bash-out 5 ``` Difference are that in the Unix shell: - There cannot be any **spaces** around the **`=`** in `x=5`. - You need a **`$` prefix** to *reference* (but not to *assign*) variables in the shell^[ Because of this, anytime you see a word/string that starts with a `$` in the shell, you can safely assume that it is a variable.]. - You need the **`echo`** command, a general command to print text, to print the value of `$x` (cf. in R). :::
### Command substitution Command substitution allows you to **store the output of a command in a variable**. Let's see an example. As you know, the `date` command will print the current date and time: ```bash date ``` ```bash-out Thu Sep 11 14:52:22 EDT 2025 ``` If we try to _store the date in a variable_ directly, it doesn't work: the literal string "date" is stored instead: ```bash today=date echo "$today" ``` ```bash-out date ``` That's why we need command substitution, which we can use by wrapping the command inside **`$()`**: ```bash today=$(date) echo "$today" ``` ```bash-out Thu Sep 11 14:54:11 EDT 2025 ```
One practical example of using command substitution is when you want to **automatically include the current date in a file name** (with "automatic" meaning that you can use the same command regardless of the date, and that you could use it in a script that you could run at any point). First, note that we can use `date +%F` to print the date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format, and omit the time: ```bash date +%F ``` ```bash-out 2025-09-07 ``` Let's use that in a command substitution: ```bash today=$(date +%F) touch README_"$today".txt ls ``` ```{.bash-out} README_2025-09-07.txt ``` ::: callout-note #### Or insert the command substitution on the fly It is even possible to do this all in one go, by using the command substitution `$(date +%F)` _directly_ in our `touch` command, rather than first assigning it to a variable: ```bash touch README_"$(date +%F)".txt ``` :::
:::{.exercise} #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Command substitution Say we wanted to count and report the number of FASTQ files in a directory in a generalized, programmatic way. To do the counting, we can run: ```bash ls *fastq | wc -l ``` ```{.bash-out} 6 ``` Now, use command substitution to store the output of the last command in a variable, and then use an `echo` command to print the following: ```bash-out-solo The dir has 6 files ``` _To be clear, `6` (or whatever the number of files ends up being) should be contained_ _in a variable and you should not be typing that character yourself!_
Click for a hint Your final `echo` command should look something like this: ```bash echo "The dir has $n_files files" ``` Now, you try to store the number of files in the variable `$n_files`.
Click for the solution ```bash n_files=$(ls *fastq | wc -l) echo "The dir has $n_files files" ``` ```{.bash-out} The dir has 6 files ``` **Note:** You don't have to quote variables _inside_ a quoted `echo` call, since it's, well, already quoted. If you _also_ quote the variables, you will in fact _unquote_ it, although that shouldn't pose a problem inside `echo` statements.
:::
## For loops Loops are another universal element of programming languages, and are used to **repeat operations**. Here, we'll only cover the most common type of loop: the `for` loop. A `for` loop _iterates_ over a collection, such as a list of files, and allows you to perform one or more actions for each element in the collection. In the example below, our "collection" is just a short list of numbers (`1`, `2`, and `3`): ```bash for a_number in 1 2 3; do echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number" echo "--------" done ``` ```bash-out In this iteration of the loop, the number is 1 -------- In this iteration of the loop, the number is 2 -------- In this iteration of the loop, the number is 3 -------- ``` The **indented lines** between `do` and `done` contain the code that is being executed _as many times as there are items in the collection_: in this case 3 times, as you can tell from the output above. What was actually run under the hood is the following: ```bash # (Don't run this) a_number=1 echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number" echo "--------" a_number=2 echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number" echo "--------" a_number=3 echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number" echo "--------" ``` Here are **two key things to understand about `for` loops**: - In each iteration of the loop, one element in the collection **is being assigned to the variable** specified after `for`. In the example above, we used `a_number` as the variable name, so that variable contained `1` when the loop ran for the first time, `2` when it ran for the second time, and `3` when it ran for the third and last time. - The loop runs sequentially for each item in the collection, and will run exactly as many times as there are items in the collection. ::: {.callout-note} #### A further explanation of `for` loop syntax On the first and last, unindented lines, `for` loops contain the following mandatory keywords: | Keyword | Purpose | |---------|-------------------------------------| | `for` | After `for`, we set the **variable name** (an arbitrary name; above we used `a_number`) | `in` | After `in`, we specify the **collection** (list of items) we are looping over | `do` | After `do`, we have one ore more lines specifying what to do with each item | `done` | Tells the shell we are done with the loop :::
#### Combining loops and globbing A very useful strategy is to loop over files with globbing, for example: ```bash for fastq_file in *fastq; do echo "Running an analysis for file $fastq_file"... # [This is where you would put additional commands to process each FASTQ file] done ``` ```bash-out Running an analysis for file sample1_R1.fastq... Running an analysis for file sample1_R2.fastq... Running an analysis for file sample2_R1.fastq... Running an analysis for file sample2_R2.fastq... Running an analysis for file sample3_R1.fastq... Running an analysis for file sample3_R2.fastq... ``` :::{.exercise} #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Exercise**: A simple loop {-} Modify the loop in our previous example to count and then print the number of lines that each FASTQ file contains: ```bash-out sample1_R1.fastq contains 0 lines sample1_R2.fastq contains 0 lines # etc. ``` _To be clear, the number of lines that the loop reports should result from_ _an actual count with `wc -l` and you should not just type `0`._
Click for the solution ```bash for fastq_file in *fastq; do n_lines=$(wc -l fastq) echo "$fastq_file contains $n_lines lines" done ``` ```bash-out sample1_R1.fastq contains 0 lines sample1_R2.fastq contains 0 lines sample2_R1.fastq contains 0 lines sample2_R2.fastq contains 0 lines sample3_R1.fastq contains 0 lines sample3_R2.fastq contains 0 lines ```
**Bonus:** Create a loop that will print: ```{.bash-out} morel is an Ohio mushroom destroying_angel is an Ohio mushroom eyelash_cup is an Ohio mushroom ```
Click for the solution ```bash for mushroom in morel destroying_angel eyelash_cup; do echo "$mushroom is an Ohio mushroom" done ``` ```bash-out morel is an Ohio mushroom destroying_angel is an Ohio mushroom eyelash_cup is an Ohio mushroom ```
:::
## The `basename` command In loops and other contexts where you are working with file names programmatically, you often have a path to a file and need to extract just the file name part from it. For example, we can think of the path `data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq` as consisting of a directory part (`data/fastq/`) and a filename part (`sample1_R1.fastq`). The **`basename` command** will extract just the filename part: ```sh basename data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq ``` ```bash-out sample1_R1.fastq ``` Optionally, it can remove a suffix too, most typically the file extension: ```bash basename data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq .fastq ``` ```bash-out sample1_R1 ```
## Renaming files with loops Sometimes, you need to rename many files in a systematic/repetitive way. This is relatively common with omics data files, as you will often have separate files for each sample, and you may have many dozens of samples. Manually renaming these one-by-one is tedious as well as extremely error-prone and not-reproducible, while doing this with code is a good example of a general task that you can apply your coding skills to. For example, maybe you have a few thousand photos that you want to rename in a systematic way? There are many different ways to rename many files in a programmatic way in the shell – admittedly none as easy as one might have hoped. Here, we'll use the `basename` command and a `for` loop. `for` loops are a verbose method for tasks like renaming, but are relatively intuitive and good to get practice with because you will use them in other contexts throughout the course. #### Creating a set of dummy files to work with We will start with creating some dummy files that represent alignments (the results of aligning reads in FASTQ files to a reference genome). These are stored in `.sam` or `.bam` files. To create many files at once, we will use a trick called "brace expansion" (because this is not a commonly used technique, I will only explain it in the optional bonus reading at the bottom of the page): ```bash cd /fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER/week03 ``` ```bash touch results/alignments/sample{01..50}.sam ``` Let's check the names of the files we created and how many there are: ```bash ls results/alignments ``` ```bash-out results/alignments/sample01.sam results/alignments/sample02.sam results/alignments/sample03.sam results/alignments/sample04.sam results/alignments/sample05.sam results/alignments/sample06.sam # [...output truncated...] ``` ```bash ls results/alignments/ | wc -l ``` ```bash-out 50 ``` Now, let's say that we noticed these files somehow have the wrong extension: they are saved as `.sam` (SAM files) but are really `.bam` (BAM files). We'll have to rename them before moving on the next step in our analysis, but it would be tedious (and error-prone! and not-reproducible!) to do this by hand. We will therefore use a loop.
#### Renaming a single file using variables To go step-by-step, I will start by showing how we could rename a single file in the way that we would have to do this in a loop --- using variables. We will actually make a _separate copy_ of the files in a separate directory, just to be safe. To start with, the original file name will be contained in a variable... ```bash oldname=results/alignments/sample01.sam ``` ...and we can also save the new name in a variable: ```bash newname=results/alignments_bam/$(basename "$oldname" .sam).bam ``` Before actually renaming, note the following trick with `echo` to just print the command instead of executing it --- that can be a really useful way to check what you're doing is correct when you're about to run a command you may be nervous about with variables: ```bash echo mv -v "$oldname" "$newname" ``` ```bash-out mv -v results/alignments/sample01.sam results/alignments_bam/sample01.bam ``` Looks good? Then we remove `echo` and rename the file (we're using the `-v` to make `mv` report what it's doing): ```bash mv -v "$oldname" "$newname" ``` ```bash-out results/alignments/sample01.sam -> results/alignments_bam/sample01.bam ```
#### Looping over all files Here's how we can loop over these files, saving each file name (one at a time) in the variable `$oldname`: ```bash for oldname in results/alignments/*.sam; do # ... done ``` Next, we assign a new name for each file: ```sh for oldname in results/alignments/*.sam; do newname=results/alignments_bam/$(basename "$oldname" .sam).bam done ``` We build and check the renaming command: ```sh for oldname in *.fastq; do newname=results/alignments_bam/$(basename "$oldname" .sam).bam echo cp -v "$oldname" "$newname" done ``` ```bash-out cp -v results/alignments/sample01.sam results/alignments_bam/sample01.bam cp -v results/alignments/sample02.sam results/alignments_bam/sample02.bam cp -v results/alignments/sample03.sam results/alignments_bam/sample03.bam cp -v results/alignments/sample04.sam results/alignments_bam/sample04.bam # [...output truncated...] ``` Finally, we actually copy and rename by removing `echo`: ```bash for oldname in *.fastq; do newname=results/alignments_bam/$(basename "$oldname" .sam).bam cp -v "$oldname" "$newname" done ``` ```bash-out ‘results/alignments/sample01.sam’ -> ‘results/alignments_bam/sample01.bam’ ‘results/alignments/sample02.sam’ -> ‘results/alignments_bam/sample02.bam’ ‘results/alignments/sample03.sam’ -> ‘results/alignments_bam/sample03.bam’ ‘results/alignments/sample04.sam’ -> ‘results/alignments_bam/sample04.bam’ # [...output truncated...] ```
